East of the Nile, where the Valley of the Kings gives way to the unforgiving wilderness of the Eastern Desert, lies a silence unbroken for millennia. It is a land of baked rock and shimmering heat, where the sun beats down with a personal malice and the very air seems to be made of fine, stinging dust. The shadows of the cliffs are sharp and black, offering the only respite in a world of blinding ochre and brilliant, pitiless blue. Here, life is a fugitive thing. A scorpion might scuttle from one rock to another; a vulture might circle on the thermals high above; but for all intents and purposes, it is a realm of death, a vast, sun-drenched tomb.

It was in this desolate landscape that two Englishmen toiled, far from the more fashionable digs of their contemporaries. The elder, Sir Reginald Hargrave, was a celebrated figure in London’s archaeological circles, a man whose name on a paper guaranteed its publication. The younger was Silas Croft, a man of twenty-five, with no name to speak of, but possessed of a brilliant, encyclopedic knowledge of ancient tongues and a fierce, scholarly ambition that burned brighter than the Egyptian sun. He was Hargrave’s assistant, his scribe, and the true engine of the expedition.

For six months they had found nothing but sand, broken pottery, and the leavings of tomb robbers millennia old. Their funds were dwindling, and the mood in the camp was sour. It was Croft who, by poring over a little-known papyrus scroll in the dead of night, divined a discrepancy in the maps of the area. He argued, with a passion that bordered on insubordination, that a small, overlooked valley had been misidentified.

Sir Reginald, weary and cynical, had at first dismissed the notion. Yet Croft’s logic was undeniable, and so, with a team of a dozen local labourers, they set out for the valley Croft had indicated. For three days they dug, finding only more rock and sand. On the evening of the third day, just as Sir Reginald was about to call a halt to the entire enterprise, one of the worker’s shovels struck not rock, but a hollow space.

A feverish excitement gripped them. By torchlight, they cleared the rubble to reveal a sealed doorway, its plaster stamp untouched. They were the first to stand before it in three thousand years. Inside, they found not a king’s ransom in gold, but something far more precious to a scholar: the intact burial chamber of a royal scribe, his personal library of tablets and scrolls miraculously preserved. And among them, in a hidden alcove Croft himself located, was a set of tablets detailing the scribe’s own system of cryptographic shorthand, a Rosetta Stone for a dialect previously unknown. It was the discovery of a lifetime.

Looking at the rows of perfect hieroglyphs, a cold and calculating look came into Sir Reginald’s eyes. He clapped a hand on his young assistant’s shoulder. “Croft, my boy,” he said, his voice thick with false emotion, “you have been working too hard. There is a mail-skiff leaving for Cairo in the morning. I want you to be on it. Take a week’s holiday. You have more than earned it.”

The young man, exhausted and overwhelmed, did not question the order. He departed the next morning, his heart swelling with pride. When he returned ten days later, the camp was gone. Back in Cairo, a penniless and ruined young man read the story in a discarded newspaper and felt something within him break, leaving behind a core of cold, patient, and everlasting ice.

His journey was a thing of nightmare. The grey dust, fine as flour, rose in choking clouds about him, filling his nostrils and coating his tongue. Thirst, a raging, maddening fiend, had taken possession of him. His head swam, and his limbs felt as heavy as lead. Again and again he fell, and for many minutes he would lie, a mere heap of rags and bone, upon the ground. Yet each time some unconquerable spirit, some deep-seated and ferocious purpose, would stir within him, and he would struggle once more to his feet and stagger onwards. Hour after hour he pressed forward, a crawling insect upon the vast face of the desert. The wisp of smoke had long since vanished with the daylight, and he was guided now only by the stars and by that grim tenacity which had become a part of his very being. The moon rose, a pale and spectral disc, and found him still toiling on, his shadow a grotesque and elongated horror flitting behind him. He had ceased to think or to feel; his progress was a purely mechanical one, the blind striving of a body which refused to grant the release that his mind so desperately craved.

It was in the deepest darkness, in those hours which precede the dawn, that he heard a sound which brought him to an abrupt halt. It was not the howl of a coyote, nor the cry of any night bird, but the low and unmistakable nickering of a horse. With the last dregs of his strength, he crept forward, his rifle held at the ready. Through the chaparral bushes he saw the flicker of a dying campfire, and around it the dark, sleeping shapes of men and animals. They were travellers, a small party camped for the night. Hope, or something akin to it, surged through him. He parted the bushes, and was about to call out, when his eyes fell upon the face of one of the sleepers, clearly illuminated by the last embers of the fire.

The man was stout and red-faced, with a thick, fair beard. He slept with his mouth agape, a picture of smug and untroubled repose. And the watcher in the bushes knew him. His name was Enoch Drebber, and he had been a junior partner in the syndicate which had financed Sir Reginald’s expedition. He had been there in Egypt; he had seen the discovery, and he had stood by in silence as the credit for it was stolen. He had taken his share of the profits and had never cast a backward glance.

A terrible change came over the face of the watcher. The weariness and despair were wiped away as if by a sponge, and in their place was a look of such cold and concentrated malignity that he seemed no longer human. The thirst, the pain, the exhaustion, all were forgotten, swallowed up by a single, all-consuming emotion which had smouldered for a decade and now burst into a smokeless flame. He did not move for a long time, but simply watched, his eyes burning with that same unnatural lustre they had held upon the mountaintop. This was not chance; it was destiny. It was the hand of a justice far older than that of man, a justice which had delivered his enemy into his hand in the heart of the great wilderness. He sank back into the shadows, not to flee, but to wait. His revenge had been a patient one, and he could afford to wait until the morning.

When the sun rose, the party of travellers awoke and began their preparations for the day. There were five of them in all, and they moved about their tasks with the easy confidence of men accustomed to the trail. The watcher, from his place of concealment, noted that a second man of the party also seemed familiar. He was a tall, thin fellow with a pinched face and nervous, darting eyes. This was Joseph Stangerson, who had served as Hargrave’s private secretary and had been the one to deliver the message sending the young scholar away on his fool’s errand to Cairo. He too had profited from the great deception. The watcher’s lips drew back from his teeth in a silent snarl. The fates were not merely kind; they were generous.

He waited until the party had breakfasted and packed their mules. Drebber, loud and boastful, was giving orders, when the watcher stepped out from the scrub, his rifle levelled. “Not another move from any of you,” he said, and his voice was a dry rasp, a sound that seemed to come from the dust itself.

The travellers froze, their faces a mixture of astonishment and fear. Drebber’s ruddy complexion turned a pasty white. “Who are you? What do you want?” he stammered.

“My name would mean nothing to you now,” the stranger replied, his burning eyes fixed upon the stout man’s face. “But you knew me once, in another land. You and he,” he added, with a slight nod towards Stangerson, who had begun to tremble violently. “I have a small matter of business to settle with you both.”

He was one man against five, and he was gaunt and starved, yet there was such an aura of deadly purpose about him that none dared to move. He held them there, under the barrel of his rifle, as the sun climbed higher in the sky. He did not speak again for a full hour, but simply stared at his two chosen victims, letting the terror build within them.

“I have journeyed a long way to find you,” he said at last, his voice still a harsh whisper. “And the justice I bring has journeyed with me. I have here,” he continued, fumbling inside his ragged blanket with his free hand, “two small pills. I took them from a collection of ancient remedies, found in a certain tomb you may recall. One contains a swift and painless poison. The other is harmless. I will place them both in my hand, and you, Enoch Drebber, will choose one. The other, I shall swallow myself. It is a game of chance. If you live, you are free to go. If you die, then justice is served. It is a fairer choice than was ever offered to me.”

He held out a small, crudely carved wooden box. He opened it, revealing two pellets of a grey, clay-like substance. Drebber stared at them, his face beaded with sweat. “This is madness!” he cried. “Stangerson! Men! He is one and we are five! Rush him!”

But no one moved. They were hypnotised by the cold fire in the stranger’s eyes, by the sheer, unholy certainty of his manner. Stangerson could only whimper, his face a mask of abject terror.

“Choose,” the stranger repeated, his voice dropping lower. “Choose, or I will choose for you, and I will not be so generous as to leave one for myself.”

With a trembling hand, Drebber reached out and took one of the pills. His eyes darted from the stranger’s face to those of his companions, searching for a rescue that would not come. The stranger, without a moment’s hesitation, picked up the remaining pill and placed it in his own mouth. He swallowed, his gaze never leaving Drebber.

For a long, silent moment, the two men stood facing each other. Then a terrible convulsion seized Drebber. His eyes bulged, his face turned a deep, apoplectic purple, and he fell to the ground, writhing in a brief and ghastly agony. A moment later, he was still.

The stranger turned his burning gaze upon Stangerson. “His luck ran out,” he said softly. “As has yours. I have no more pills for you, Joseph Stangerson. Your fate will be a different one. I will hunt you. You may run now, as fast and as far as you are able. But I will find you. Whether it be in a month, or a year, or ten years from now, I will find you. And when I do, there will be no game of chance.”

He gave a slight, almost imperceptible nod towards the other three travellers, who had stood like statues throughout the terrible ordeal. “Your business is not with me. Go.”

As if released from a spell, the three men scrambled for their mules, and without a backward glance, fled into the desert, leaving Stangerson alone with the corpse of his companion and the terrifying figure of his judge. Stangerson stared for a moment, his mind unhinged by fear, and then, with a choked sob, he turned and ran, a frantic, stumbling flight into the vast and empty plains.

The stranger watched him go until he was a small, dark speck in the distance. He did not follow. He knelt beside the body of Enoch Drebber and, dipping his finger into a small cut on his own hand, he scrawled a single word in the dust beside the dead man’s head. It was an ancient word, a word for divine retribution. Then, taking up the dead man’s waterskin and a small portion of his food, he turned his face towards the west and began to walk, his step no longer the faltering gait of a dying man, but the steady, indefatigable tread of an avenging angel. His name was Silas Croft, and his work was only half-finished. He had a promise to keep, and a long journey to London ahead of him.

“No,” said Holmes, holding up a hand. “That would be to play their game. A cordon of uniformed constables would send our quarry scattering like frightened pigeons, and they would surely silence the Professor before they fled. They are desperate men, Mr. Blackwood, to go to such lengths. No, we must meet them on our own terms. I shall go to St. Bartholomew’s this evening. And I shall go alone.”

“Alone, Holmes? That is madness!” I protested. “It is an obvious trap!”

“Precisely, my dear Watson,” he replied, a dangerous gleam in his eyes. “It is a trap. And they have made the amateur’s mistake of assuming the cheese is more intelligent than the mouse.” He turned to our client. “Mr. Blackwood, your part in this is done. I must ask you to return to your home and speak of this to no one. If my suspicions are correct, you may be under observation. Watson, you will come with me. We have some arrangements to make. Our friends of the Serpent are expecting a scholar to arrive at six. I flatter myself that we can provide them with a rather more vigorous reception than they anticipate.”
